title: Share one multiplier across all RV32M multiply variants
motivation:
The combinational ALU currently instantiates three separate 32-by-32 products for
signed-signed, unsigned-unsigned, and signed-unsigned multiplication. Only one
multiply instruction can execute at a time, so the duplicated multiplier fabric
consumes scarce LUT/DSP and routing resources without increasing throughput.

title: Decouple fetch with a two-entry instruction FIFO
motivation:
The current frontend ties the fetch PC directly to backend stalls. Whenever a
data-memory operation freezes EX/MEM, an otherwise-ready instruction-memory
cycle is discarded; later random instruction-memory backpressure then creates
another bubble. A shallow fetch queue can use those idle frontend cycles to
build slack without adding a cache or changing architectural behavior.

title: Static backward-branch and direct-JAL predictor
motivation:
Every taken branch, JAL, and JALR currently redirects only when it reaches EX,
flushing the younger fetch/decode work. CoreMark contains loop-closing backward
branches and direct calls, so this repeated control penalty reduces iterations
per cycle. A decode-light static predictor can remove most of those bubbles
without a BHT, BTB, or return stack, which is important because the current core
is already close to its LUT target and fitness also depends on FPGA Fmax.

The ALU expresses signed and unsigned quotient and remainder operations as
separate wide division and modulo operators. Since only one RV32M operation
executes at a time, parallel signed and unsigned divider fabrics add LUT and
routing pressure without increasing throughput, much like the duplicated
multipliers removed by the previous winning micro-optimization.

load/store, branch, and multiply operations. The failed frontend structures

title: Gate load-use hazards by actual source operands
motivation:
The load-use detector compares a pending load destination against both raw
source-register bitfields of every following instruction. Several RV32IM
formats do not read one or either of those fields, so immediate bits or a
destination field can accidentally match the load destination and insert a
needless pipeline bubble. CoreMark contains frequent loads followed by
immediate arithmetic, further loads, and control-flow instructions, making
these false dependencies a direct IPC loss under the existing bus-stall model.

The current five-stage pipeline carries a wide MEM/WB payload for every

motivation:
The exact-target one-instruction replay buffer is the only predictor structure
that has improved fitness, but its replace-on-every-miss policy lets a single
cold taken backward branch evict a frequently reused loop-head instruction.

timing cost than CoreMark recovered, so replacement policy is the remaining
way to improve effective coverage without widening the replay datapath.

title: Replay-aligned source-qualified load-use hazard
motivation:
The load-use detector treats both register-shaped instruction fields as consumed
sources for every opcode. Accidental matches therefore insert bubbles after loads
even when the following instruction does not read rs1 or rs2. The previous rs2-only
qualification attempt targeted this useful CPI opportunity but became incorrect
when branch replay replaced the live IF instruction without replacing the opcode
used by hazard detection.

title: Uniform two-stage execute pipeline
motivation:
Routed timing evidence and the last structural experiment both identify the
single-cycle ID/EX-to-EX/MEM multiply path as the remaining Fmax limiter.
Prior multiplier sidecars tried to shorten it with operation-specific busy
state and global interlocks, but those controls burdened ordinary cycles and
the completion mux still sat on the long arithmetic path. A pipeline stage
used uniformly by every instruction can provide a true timing cut without
dispatch, busy, or completion arbitration.

title: One-bit hysteretic replay-entry replacement
motivation:
The confirmed backward-branch replay entry improves this core, but every
exact-target miss immediately displaces the resident loop head. In nested
loops, an infrequent outer-loop backedge can therefore evict the frequently
reused inner-loop target just before execution returns to that inner loop.
A second candidate or victim tag is too expensive on this FPGA, but a single
replacement-protection bit can distinguish a proven hot entry without adding
another wide comparator or target register.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add one-bit replacement hysteresis to the existing exact-target replay entry.
Set the protection bit whenever the resident entry hits. On the first miss

or combinational logic to io_imemAddr. Replay remains EX-confirmed, so wrong
instructions are never injected and architectural control flow, stalls,
traps, RVFI ordering, and the nret=1 interface remain unchanged.

title: Immediate-sign backward replay qualification
motivation:
The confirmed one-entry replay buffer still classifies a resolved branch as
backward with a full 32-bit unsigned comparison of branch_target against the
branch PC. That comparison sits in the EX-to-replay qualification cone and is
redundant for ordinary RV32 B-type control flow because the sign bit of the
decoded branch displacement already states whether its offset is negative.
The earlier direction-agnostic experiment removed this comparator but admitted
forward branches, whose replacements thrashed the useful backward-loop entry.

motivation:
The current Fmax limiter is the single-cycle path from ID/EX through the
mapper-native 32x32 product into EX/MEM. The previous added execute stage
sat after that product and therefore duplicated pipeline state without
shortening the critical arithmetic cone. A useful structural retime must
place its register inside multiplication while keeping multiply-specific
control away from the ordinary fetch and decode stall paths.
